vignette:
He is 24, a South Eastern Asian man who works as a painter, and when he first talks about the relationship he does not begin with fear. He begins with color. He says he used to come home with his hands still stained in cobalt or ochre, and his boyfriend would laugh and call him careless when he touched a doorframe and left a mark. In the beginning, that laughter feels intimate, like being seen. They move quickly into each other's routines. He paints walls and apartments during the day, sometimes murals on commission when work is steady, and in the evenings he brings home takeout, scrolls through design ideas, and listens to his partner talk about plans for the future. He remembers feeling lucky that someone wanted him so completely.

The first time he is hit, they are in the kitchen of the apartment they share. It starts with an accusation that he is flirting with a client because he came home late from a job. He tries to explain that the paint had not dried evenly and he had to stay and fix it. His partner steps closer, voice rising, and before he understands what is happening, he is slapped hard across the face. He goes quiet. What shocks him most is not the pain but how quickly the room changes. The kitchen light seems too bright. He hears the refrigerator humming. His partner begins crying almost immediately, saying he was pushed too far, saying it would not happen again. He believes him, or wants to.

After that, he starts measuring his words. He checks his phone before he walks in the door and deletes messages that could be misread. He sends photos from job sites so there will be proof of where he is. He tells himself this is temporary, that stress is making everything worse. But the violence becomes part of the rhythm of the relationship. He is shoved into walls, grabbed by the jaw, once punched in the ribs when he tries to leave during an argument. The worst incident happens after a weekend job painting a café. He returns home exhausted and still smelling faintly of solvent. His partner has been drinking and is angry that he did not answer his phone while on a ladder. When he says he cannot keep apologizing for working, his partner throws a mug that shatters near his feet, then tackles him into the edge of a table. He remembers curling inward, arms over his head, while his partner kicks at his side. He remembers thinking, very calmly, that he should not let his face get damaged because he has work in the morning.

He does go to work the next day. He tells his boss he slipped carrying supplies. While rolling primer onto a bedroom wall, he feels a wave of unreality, as if he is watching his body move from a distance. The smell of fresh paint, usually grounding and familiar, makes his stomach turn because it reminds him of that night at the café and the drive home. In the weeks that follow, he startles when customers come up behind him. If someone raises a voice in a hallway or drops a metal tray, his chest seizes and he feels the urge to duck. At night he lies awake listening for footsteps, even after the relationship ends and he is sleeping in his cousin's spare room. When he does sleep, he wakes sweating from dreams in which he cannot move his arms or call for help.

He has not told many people what happened. He notices how easily others assume that because he is a young man, because he works with his hands, because he stayed, it could not have been that bad. Even with his current partner, who is gentle and patient, he finds himself bracing. If his boyfriend reaches too quickly to touch his shoulder from behind, he jerks away before he can stop himself, then feels ashamed. During disagreements he goes blank. He says it is as if his mind shuts a door and leaves him standing outside it. Later he replays conversations over and over, searching for the moment when things could have turned dangerous, even when they never did.

His world has grown smaller in ways he does not like admitting. He avoids the neighborhood where he used to live. He has stopped taking certain apartment jobs if they are in buildings similar to the one he shared with his ex, especially narrow walk-ups with dim stairwells and thin kitchen spaces. He prefers to work with music on because silence makes too much room for memory. Some days painting still gives him relief: the focus of taping edges, the satisfaction of covering a damaged wall with clean color. Other days he catches sight of bruised purples or deep reds on a palette and feels his throat tighten.

In the present, he speaks carefully, often minimizing before correcting himself. He says he is "not that kind of person," then pauses, frowns, and says he does not even know what that means. He wants closeness and is frightened by it. He is tired of scanning rooms, tired of waking as if someone has called his name, tired of feeling his body react before his mind can catch up. What stays with him most is not only the memory of being hurt, but how ordinary everything looked while it was happening: the kitchen light, the drying paint on his hands, the next day's work waiting for him as if nothing had changed.
